evidence: DeformX models DLOs as Cosserat rods; the framework is a direct application of Cosserat rod theory.
Rod engine uses a discrete Cosserat formulation in the Bergou-Audoly DER family (vertices + per-edge SO(3) frames).
Object class targeted by the framework.
Sim-to-real transfer of policies trained in DeformX is the paper's central empirical claim.
Paper proposes the multi-rate Cosserat-rod + Isaac Sim co-simulation pattern; this is the paper's primary architectural contribution.
Rope-swinging hit-target task on UR5e: DeformX vs. Isaac linked-capsule baseline reduces real-world tip-to-goal error from 15.1/25.9/30.4 cm to 6.6/7.3/5.8 cm across three targets, n=10 each.
Paper explicitly proposes and names the Iterative Residual Policy (IRP) framework as its primary contribution.
Paper introduces the Delta Dynamics Network as the specific architectural component that enables IRP.
Real-world results: 1.3-5.5 cm tip-to-goal error across 7 unseen ropes and 2 unseen robot embodiments at iteration 9.
IRP outperforms SysID/SysID_GT in simulation extrapolation and outperforms OptSim oracle on real ropes with un-modeled physics.
Rope is a 1D deformable linear object; cloth manipulation is included as 2D extension.
Core empirical claim space — IRP closes the sim-to-real gap via online adaptation rather than randomization or sysid.
Delta dynamics is structurally a learned Jacobian of trajectories with respect to action perturbations; ILC connection in related work.
Sample-and-evaluate action selection at each iteration is structurally one-step MPC with a learned model.
Visual feedback (rasterized rope-tip trajectory image) drives action refinement across iterations.
Implicit randomization across the (length, density) training grid acts as the simulator-side variation.
MuJoCo's linked-capsule rope (25 capsules) and cloth (13x13 grid) is the simulator's DLO representation.
TossingBot coins the term 'Residual Physics' in Sec. IV-V and demonstrates it on action-space release-velocity residuals.
TossingBot defines the parameterized throwing primitive (release position + velocity, geometric simplifications reducing to scalar release magnitude).
TossingBot uses a closed-form ballistic action prior both as a residual base and as a 128-channel input feature, exemplifying the physics-informed-action-prior pattern.

TossingBot is the source paper for this claim — provides the empirical evidence (84.7% / 82.3% real-world throw success, 87.2% / 83.9% generalization to unseen targets) cited by the claim's evidence field.
Pixel-wise grasp affordance prediction is the perception-to-grasp interface; grasping is the upstream foundation for the joint grasping-throwing learning.
Trains in PyBullet simulation, deploys on real UR5; sim-to-real is structural to the experimental design.
Pick-from-bin + throw of arbitrary geometry sits in the contact-rich manipulation regime; ballistic prior cannot model contact-induced offsets and the residual learns these.
Random object color and placement during training; light DR for visual robustness.
Throw and grasp primitives use a stable, collision-free IK solver to execute the planned end-effector trajectories.
DEFORM extends DER with autodiff (DDER) and residual learning
DER (DEFORM's backbone) is a discrete differential geometry formulation of Cosserat rod dynamics
object class targeted by DEFORM
DEFORM's inextensibility correction is a momentum-preserving modification of PBD
compared as DLO-modeling alternative; identifies stiffness/instability issues
discussed as accurate-but-too-slow alternative
DEFORM is calibrated against MoCap and deployed on real robots
bi-level autodiff via Theseus implicit differentiation
training and parameter ID via gradient-based optimization
DEFORM defines DDER as the differentiable reformulation of DER
DEFORM inserts a DNN residual inside the DDER integrator step
DEFORM introduces the mass-ratio scaling that makes the PBD inextensibility correction momentum-preserving
DEFORM's experiments are the supporting evidence for this claim
DEFORM's DDER is a methodological component that could plug into DeformX's Cosserat rod engine; both target sim-to-real DLO modeling
both use residual physics — TossingBot at policy level, DEFORM at simulator integrator level
both use residual physics for dynamic DLO problems; IRP at policy/goal level, DEFORM at simulator level
both target DER-based DLO simulation with parameter identification from real data
both are differentiable physics for deformables; DaXBench is a broader benchmark suite, DEFORM is a single-object-class simulator with a residual learning specialization
both target dynamic DLO sim-to-real; Real2Sim2Real uses self-supervised data, DEFORM uses MoCap-supervised differentiable physics
both target dynamic cable manipulation; Lost Arc is a fixed-endpoint self-supervised learning approach without an explicit physics model
RopeDreamer is a learned recurrent latent dynamics model for ropes; an alternative learning-based DLO dynamics paradigm to DEFORM's hybrid
task-conditioned DLO manipulation; complements DEFORM's dynamics-modeling focus
IPA implicitly bakes physics into a policy; DEFORM explicitly uses differentiable physics — complementary instantiations of physics-informed dynamic DLO control
ETH whole-body throwing is dynamic manipulation but for rigid objects; complementary to dynamic DLO modeling
Flying Knot ILC targets dynamic 3D DLO manipulation with iterative learning control rather than differentiable physics
SoftMimicGen is automated demonstration generation; complements DEFORM's simulator-side calibration
RAPiD adapts particle-based dynamics to new deformables; complementary cross-DLO generalization angle that DEFORM does not address
model-based RL self-curriculum; DEFORM provides the kind of accurate model the curriculum could exploit
Wiggle&Go is zero-shot system identification for dynamic deformables; targets the cross-object generalization gap DEFORM does not close
Free-end-cable / dynamic planar manipulation; complements 3D dynamic DLO modeling
Adapts the bending/twisting energies and quasi-static twist treatment of Bergou et al.'s Discrete Elastic Rods (DER) into MuJoCo via a force-lever conversion to generalized coordinates.
DER discretizes Cosserat rod theory (paper drops stretch and shear, retains bending and twisting); cited as the parent theory of the rod model used here.
Object class targeted by the simulator and the parameter identification pipeline.
Motivation: provide an accurate MuJoCo-native DLO simulation that warm-starts sim-to-real workflows and reduces real-data requirements for downstream learning.
Discussed and rejected as the alternative DLO representation; mass-spring tuning loses physical interpretability.
Discussed as a visually-plausible alternative DLO representation that lacks physical accuracy at large deformations.
Defines the force-lever conversion of DER Cartesian centerline forces to MuJoCo ball-joint torques, plus quasi-static centerline-twist treatment, as the architectural mechanism of the paper.
Three-way validation: localized helical buckling, Michell's instability, and 4-pose real-vs-sim shape comparison on three DLOs, all favoring the adapted DER model over MuJoCo's native cable plugin.
Object class targeted: cables (DLOs) on a planar surface.
Real2Sim2Real is one specific recipe for the broader sim-to-real transfer problem.
Paper explicitly contrasts R2S2R against domain randomization as the alternate sim-to-real strategy.
PyBullet cable model is a chain of capsule rigid bodies with 6-DOF spring constraints — a discrete mass-spring instantiation.
Differential Evolution and Bayesian Optimization are the optimization machinery for Real2Sim parameter tuning.
Paper names and instantiates the three-step Real2Sim2Real pipeline.
Empirically establishes DE-based simulator parameter tuning for cable dynamics, beating Bayesian Optimization in Sim2Sim and serving as the workhorse Real2Sim engine.
Per-cable median tip-error 8/12/14% of cable length on PRC across three cables, 75 trials each. Mixed-data NN policy beats pure-real and pure-sim baselines.
DIDP framework: full-system reduced-order diffusion policy with IL+TO pretraining and physics-informed test-time adaptation; defining contribution of the paper
PITA mechanism: posterior-score augmentation with differentiable physics loss (DDP) plus kinematic boundary condition (KBC), with adaptation restricted to the final projection layer
DIDP wraps the GVS reduced-order rod parameterization (Mathew et al. 2025) for the simulator backbone and to express the differentiable forward kinematics used in PITA
DIDP is built on the goal-conditioned diffusion policy paradigm (Chi et al. 2023); replaces the action-only state with full-system reduced-order state and adds physics-guided test-time adaptation
Object class: 1D rope as a continuum DLO
GVS reduces the Cosserat-rod continuum dynamics into a finite-DoF strain-basis representation
IL+TO learning strategy: imitation learning from 55k expert trajectories provides the diffusion policy's pretraining signal
IL pretraining stage uses behavior cloning on demonstrated full-system trajectories (matched against L_diff)
Reports the headline DIDP results (84.3%@5cm, 20.8%@1cm, 3.6cm mean) on the 3D rope-whipping benchmark
Reports ablations: PITA (DDP+KBC) lifts @5cm from 80.0% to 84.3% over no-TTA baseline; project-only adaptation outperforms full-network finetune at lower cost
Paper frames the dynamic-DLO problem as needing physics-grounded sim-only training with sim-to-real implications, though no real-robot transfer is demonstrated
Pullback tube acceleration is a constrained convex optimization solved at >1 kHz over a short horizon; conceptually a real-time receding-horizon controller (Section IIIC, Tube-CVX program).
Three-layer stack mixes model-free RL (PPO nominal + residual) with a model-based optimizer (pullback tube QP).
Standard sim-to-real techniques applied to both nominal and residual training stages, including domain randomization, observation noise, and symmetry augmentation (Section III-D).
Actuator networks, observation noise, and symmetry augmentation listed as standard sim-to-real techniques applied; residual policy explicitly flagged as suffering a sim-to-real gap.

Gripper-object detachment uncertainty (50-100 ms detach window from screw drive fingers + variable normal-force vanishing time) is a contact-uncertainty problem central to the paper's release-time model.
Robotiq 2f140 prehensile gripper used; release-time uncertainty is bounded by the 50 ms gripper dwell time and material deformation.
The 400 Hz residual policy on top of a frozen 100 Hz nominal is named and contributed in this paper (Section III-B High-frequency Residual Policy and contribution bullet 2 in introduction).
Pullback Tube Acceleration is named in Section III-C as the closed-loop variant of Liu and Billard's open-loop tube acceleration; the convex Tube-CVX program is the paper's contribution.

Paper formulates whole-body prehensile throwing as time-dependent EE state tracking on the goal manifold of object flight; first reported instance of prehensile whole-body throwing with quantified hardware accuracy (conclusion).

40 timed throws across 4 ground-target locations (4 m and 6 m forward, ±0.5 m lateral); mean landing error 0.276 m at 6 m, 0.429 m at 4 m for full stack vs 0.685 m / 0.710 m for nominal-only baseline; 49.5% accuracy improvement; 1500-condition simulation grid shows monotonic landing error reduction with pullback control rate; human comparison: robot 56.8% vs humans 15.2% (Section IV).

Pinocchio inverse-dynamics analysis of 5 throws at 10 m/s horizontal velocity: legged base contributes 51.7 N*m*s of angular momentum and 46.3 J of work prior to release; 53.4% higher angular impulse than tabletop manipulator running same joint trajectory; base remains stationary at low velocities and tilts as commanded velocity grows (Section IV-C, Fig. base_motion).

IPA paper introduces and embodies fixed-probe implicit system identification: a predefined high-acceleration probe action whose response trajectory map is fed directly into the action regressor, with no explicit physics-parameter estimation.
IPA explicitly names the rope+rigid-payload heterogeneous system as a target regime distinct from pure-DLO and pure-rigid-body manipulation, and structures both task and policy around it.
IPA's two-stage policy reaches 72.5% SR on 50 simulated O2T cases and 62.5% SR on 8 real-world cases without real-world training; ablations isolate the implicit-sysID encoder as the dominant lever.

IPA explicitly contrasts iterative residual approaches (IRP, TossingBot) with implicit-sysID-then-commit, and shows that a single SysID probe + one-shot regression beats SQ-RND (3-trial squeezing-bounds sampler standing in for iterative-feedback baselines) on heterogeneous DLO+rigid transport.
Paper introduces and names Task-Level ILC for deformable-object manipulation; the core algorithm is the paper's principal contribution.
Paper formalizes the critical-point objective as the cost-design choice that makes Task-Level ILC succeed on the flying knot; ablation against equal-weighting confirms necessity.
Inverse model is implemented as a QP via Drake + Clarabel with linearized rope dynamics, joint position/velocity/acceleration/torque constraints, and a critical-point error term.

Rope is modeled as a 3D serial chain of point masses connected by fixed-distance constraints with per-joint bending stiffness and damping — a mass-spring chain with bending. End-mass is tunable, total of 5 free parameters.

Section 'Learning Across Rope Types' and 'Learned Command Success Rate': 7-rope evaluation, 100% success within 10 trials per rope, 40-trial repeatability check shows 0 failures on the converged command.

Section 'Transfer of Learned Command' and Figure transfer_learning: cross-rope transfer with most pairs needing 2-5 additional trials; rope 7 is sometimes zero-shot; ropes 5/6 → 2/3 fail in 10 trials.

IRP (Chi 2022) is the conceptual ancestor: same observation that dynamic rope tasks are repeatable and benefit from trial-to-trial command refinement. IRP learns the residual via deep nets on simulated data; this work replaces that with a one-shot QP and skips the simulator entirely while staying in the same problem framing.

Real2Sim2Real (Lim 2022) is cited as an alternative path for sample-efficient dynamic rope manipulation: fit a simulator from physical rollouts and plan. Section 2.2 contrasts both approaches; Section 6.1 argues Task-Level ILC eliminates the need for a simulator-fit-and-plan pipeline.

Lost-Arc (Zhang 2024) is cited as a contrasting line: large-scale self-supervised data on dynamic rope arcing motions. Section 2.2 places this paper alongside IRP and Lost-Arc as 'system models learned with large-scale simulated data,' arguing Model-Based ILC eliminates that need.

Rope is one of four deformable object classes benchmarked; the JAX simulator's rope manipulation tasks (Push-Rope, Whip-Rope) and sim-to-real real-robot evaluation (Push-Rope on Kinova Gen3) directly target DLOs.

DaX models cloth dynamics with a mass-spring system (mesh-based) — paper Section 3.1 / appendix sec:object_model. Rationale: cloth undergoes only limited deformation, so the simpler mass-spring model is preferred over MPM.
Sim-to-real claim: CEM-MPC + DaX deployed on a Kinova Gen3 for Push-Rope produces real-robot trajectories that closely track DaX-predicted next states (paper Section 4.4 + appendix sim2real).
Imitation Learning is one of the three benchmarked algorithm paradigms; baselines include Transporter (non-differentiable) and ILD (differentiable physics).
CEM-MPC and Diff-CEM-MPC use the simulator as predictive model and plan via cross-entropy elite resampling; this is the model-based-RL/MPC family.
Comparison with FEM-based DOM simulators (DiffSim) is part of Table 1 simulator_comparison; FEM is the alternative continuum baseline.
Transporter networks (one of two IL baselines benchmarked) is a behavioral-cloning style imitation learner over pick-and-place affordances.

DaXBench is the canonical instantiation of the multi-object differentiable DOM benchmark pattern: JAX-batched MLS-MPM (rope/liquid) + mass-spring (cloth) + 9 tasks + 8 algorithms across planning/IL/RL.
DaXBench Table RL_results (Whip-Rope): APG 0.83 ± 0.01, SHAC 0.66 ± 0.03, PPO 0.25 ± 0.10 over 20 seeds. APG dominates by 3.3x over PPO and 1.26x over SHAC.

DaXBench Whip-Rope: APG 0.83 / SHAC 0.66 vs CEM-MPC 0.34 / Diff-MPC 0.37 / Diff-CEM-MPC 0.33. JAX simulator achieves 128 batched rollouts of 80 timesteps (forward + backward) in ~3 s on 4 x 2080-Ti GPUs (paper Section sec:jax).
Wiggle-and-Go targets dynamic manipulation of ropes (DLOs) — the object class is foundational to the contribution.
The full pipeline is sim-to-real: phi is trained entirely in simulation, CMA-ES trajectory optimization runs in Drake, and only the wiggle and final task rollout execute on the real xArm 7.
Phi-NN is trained with three forms of domain randomization (calibration noise, anisotropic tracking noise, trajectory padding) plus progressive curriculum masking to bridge the sim-to-real gap.
CMA-ES (Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy) is the trajectory optimizer used by the Go stage to plan the task-specific 3-waypoint joint-space spline.

Wiggle and Go! introduces the task-agnostic system identification pattern: one safe wiggle observation + a TCN-MLP network predicts a 9-D rope-parameter vector that is then reused across point-striking, lobbing, and draping without retraining the identifier.

Section IV reports 3.55 cm 3D-target-striking accuracy in real with phi-NN-predicted parameters across 600 rollouts on 4 in-domain ropes vs. 15.29 cm for non-system-parameter-informed baseline. Cross-validated by simulation results (Table tab:sim-full) and motion-fidelity metrics (Pearson 0.95, 5.4 cm/frame).

Wiggle-and-Go positions itself explicitly against IRP-class methods in the introduction and Related Work, arguing that 5-10 iteration retries are dangerous when failures are unrecoverable. The 3.55 cm zero-retry result substantiates the design statement, but the paper does not run a head-to-head comparison.

Wiggle-and-Go's rope simulator follows Lim et al.'s ball-joint chain parameterization (Section III.A.1: 'we represent ropes in simulation using the link, ball joint chains, following Lim et al.') and the lead-weight-at-tip modeling. The conceptual extension: replace 50-iteration DE simulator-tuning + many real trajectories with a single forward pass of a TCN-MLP from one wiggle, and lift from 2D planar casting to 3D point striking + lobbing + draping. Jeffrey Ichnowski is shared between the two papers (Berkeley->CMU lineage).

Section 3 (Problem Definition) introduces a parametric trajectory function f_A : R^3 -> A that takes a 3D apex point and produces a complete arm trajectory; Section 4 (Method) instantiates it as a min-jerk QP. The contribution list explicitly names INDy and the parameterized minimum-jerk trajectories as new contributions.

INDy outperforms fixed-apex and human-task-specific apex baselines across vaulting (81.7 vs 51.7/66.7), knocking (65.0 vs 36.7/56.7), weaving (60.0 vs 15.0/15.0), with cross-cable transfer to four other cables of similar length without retraining (Table III). 5 cables, 3 difficulty tiers, 60 trials/tier physical evaluation.
The paper studies dynamic manipulation of cables (DLOs) and uses 'cable' to refer to any 1D deformable object with low stiffness.
Section 4.1 trains the deployed policy via behavior cloning on self-collected (image, apex) pairs, with MSE loss and the reparameterization trick over a multivariate Gaussian output.
Section 4.1 frames the approach as deep imitation learning over a self-collected dataset of successful (observation, apex) pairs.

Section 4 uses a Blender Featherstone simulator to find the base apex action that bootstraps real-robot data collection; Section 6 reports a sim-to-real correlation study showing ~50% of real failures succeed in simulation under matched settings.

Introduces a 4-parameter polar two-arc + wrist-rotation primitive (theta_1, theta_2, r_2, psi) that defines the trainable action manifold; coverage increases from ~66% (without psi) to ~80% (with psi) of the reachable semicircle.

Applies the three-stage Real2Sim2Real recipe (autonomous real data collection + DE simulator tuning + supervised forward-dynamics training on D_sim+D_real) from the predecessor Lim et al. 2022 to the free-end cable setting; same pipeline pattern, PyBullet capsule chain instead of Isaac Gym FleX-segmented.

Uses scipy.optimize.differential_evolution with best1bin strategy (CR=0.7, F in [0.5,1.0]) to minimize average waypoint L2 distance between simulated and real cable trajectories across 60 training trajectories per cable; tunes 10 PyBullet parameters per cable. Reduces final endpoint L2 error from 25-35% (PyBullet defaults) to 12-15% per cable.
Per-cable median tip error 22%/24%/34% of cable length on three cables (160 trials each); the source paper for this claim.

Cross-paper comparison: free-end planar at 22-34% median tip error vs. predecessor PRC at 8-14% under the same Real2Sim2Real pipeline pattern and per-cable-length normalization; 2-3x worse on the free-end / longer-trajectory setting.
Provides the 8-14% per-cable median tip error baseline against which the free-end paper's 22-34% is compared; same lab, same pipeline pattern, same per-cable-length normalization.
Cable is the canonical 1D deformable linear object; the paper uses 'cable' as a generic term for ropes, wires, threads.
DE-tunes-PyBullet then trains on D_sim plus fine-tunes on D_real; the entire pipeline is a sim-to-real transfer pattern.
Uses a standard IK solver to convert polar end-effector trajectories (r,theta,psi) into UR5 joint trajectories at the robot's control cycle.
Differential Evolution and grid-search are derivative-free black-box optimization machinery applied to simulator parameter tuning and test-time action selection respectively.
PyBullet capsule-chain cable model uses 6-DOF spring constraints linking consecutive capsules; this is a discrete twist/bend mass-spring instantiation.
Forward dynamics MLP is trained via supervised regression on (action, observed-tip-position) pairs from grid-sampled trajectories; methodologically a behavioral-cloning variant.

Direct successor of Lim et al. 2022. Same Berkeley AUTOLAB lab, explicit citation in introduction and related work as the immediate predecessor (cite{harry_rope_2021} is fixed-end; this paper extends the PRC pipeline to free-end). Re-uses Real2Sim2Real recipe and DE simulator tuning, replaces 5-parameter action with 4-parameter polar two-arc + wrist primitive, switches Isaac Gym FleX-segmented for PyBullet only.
Trains all visuomotor policies via maximum-likelihood Behavioral Cloning on the SoftMimicGen-generated dataset (Sec. III.A).
Pipeline output is a large imitation-learning dataset; policies are imitation-learned.
Diffusion Policy is one of two visuomotor policy classes evaluated on SoftMimicGen-generated data (the other is BC-RNN-GMM); see Sec. V.
Image-conditioned visuomotor policies trained on generated data bypass non-rigid registration at inference time (Sec. IV.D).
Rope, surgical thread, and tissue tasks are core DLO instances in the simulation suite.
Reports zero-shot sim-to-real and sim-real co-training results on three real-world deformable tasks (Table 3).
Threading, whipping, and folding tasks all involve sustained or impulsive contact.
Broader initial-state randomization at generation time is the analog of policy-training-time domain randomization.

SoftMimicGen explicitly defines and introduces the non-rigid-registration-based automated demonstration generation mechanism for deformable manipulation as the paper's primary contribution (Secs. III-IV).

70-100% generation success across 10 Isaac Lab tasks spanning four embodiments and four object classes, including dynamic Jenga whipping, surgical threading, and bimanual folding; 49/50 vs. 4/50 head-to-head against vanilla MimicGen on Franka rope U-shaping; sim-real co-training improves over real-only baseline (Tables 1-3).
First author and corresponding author of SoftMimicGen.
RopeDreamer's target object class is the DLO (rope, cable, suture); the paper formalizes the DLO state and dynamics modeling task.
Forward kinematics with fixed link length is used to recover Cartesian segment positions from the quaternionic kinematic-chain state representation.
RSSM (Recurrent State Space Model) is the canonical world-model backbone from the Dreamer/PlaNet line of model-based RL, adapted here as a DLO dynamics model.

Paper introduces the Quaternionic Kinematic RSSM with dual-decoder architecture combining quaternion-based DLO state representation, RSSM latent dynamics, and separate reconstruction/prediction decoders.

MuJoCo benchmark over 500 50-step rollouts: 40.52% RMSE reduction at t=50 vs. GA-Net S baseline, 31.17% inference-time reduction; topology fidelity (Gauss-code) holds 38-65% across horizon while baselines drop below 10% by t=30; ablation isolates long-horizon stability to RSSM rather than the quaternionic representation alone.

RAPiD introduces RMA-style privileged-particle teacher-student adaptation: Phase I privileged Shape+Dynamics encoders trained with RL, Phase II non-privileged adaptation modules trained by L1 regression onto the frozen embeddings.

82.5% aggregate real-world success on 40 rollouts across two TIAGo deformable mobile-manipulation tasks with unseen object categories; 65+ pp margin over DDOD/DMfD baselines; ablations support shape-adaptation as the load-bearing component.
1D rope/cable manipulation in 1D_Inserting task.
Sim-only training on OmniGibson, zero-shot deployment on real TIAGo.
Depth-image-conditioned full-DOF action policy is the deployed agent.
Implicit randomization across 20 deformable categories in simulation training.
Phase II adaptation modules are L1-regressed onto privileged-teacher embeddings (BC-shaped distillation).
Both 1D_Inserting and 2D_Covering require grasping the deformable object as a subroutine.
Object class: paper targets DLO shape control with two robots manipulating both ends of a rope.
Builds on the MBPO branched-rollout framework (Janner 2019) using a Bi-LSTM ensemble dynamics model and SAC policy training.
The small-deformation stage is exactly Jacobian-based shape servoing on the rope shape descriptor.
Small-deformation controller is an online Jacobian-based visual servo with weighted least-squares Jacobian updates.
Online weighted-least-squares Jacobian estimation (Zhu 2018 / Jin 2019) drives the small-deformation stage.
Headline empirical claim: zero-shot deployment of MuJoCo-trained policy to three real DLOs achieves 30/30 success.

Paper proposes the imagined-evaluation curriculum loop with intermediate-difficulty filtering and Weighted Farthest Point Sampling under epistemic-uncertainty weighting; this is the paper's primary methodological contribution.

Real-world experiments: 30/30 zero-shot success across three DLOs (electric wire, USB cable, braided cotton rope) with 5 straight + 5 diverse cases each; avg min err 1.99/2.06 mm vs. 13–61 mm for MPC, Visual-Servo, RL-Only baselines; policy trained purely in MuJoCo, no real-world fine-tuning.

DIDP positions itself as the 3D extension beyond IRP-style 2D rope-tip tasks; same task class, different action representation (full reduced-order joint trajectory via diffusion policy vs IRP's parameterized swing primitive).
IPA replaces IRP's per-trial iterative residual loop with up-front implicit system identification + one-shot goal-conditioned action prediction; explicit anti-IRP design choice.
Wiggle-and-Go uses task-agnostic sysID + Drake CMA-ES trajectory optimization for zero-shot 3D rope-tip striking — explicitly contrasts IRP's learned iterative residual on the same target-class task.

Both target arbitrary 3D rope-tip points (Wiggle-and-Go on real xArm 7; DIDP in 20-DoF reduced-order Cosserat sim); the two papers stake out the real-hardware vs sim-only ends of the same 3D rope-strike problem.

Sister Berkeley AUTOLAB papers from ICRA 2022 — both self-supervised learning of dynamic cable manipulation on UR5; Lost-Arc fixed-endpoint with 3D apex-point representation, Real2Sim2Real free-tip planar casting.

Both use residual physics over an analytic prior for goal-conditioned throwing; ETH-WB-Throw generalizes TossingBot's scalar release-velocity residual to a 100Hz nominal MPC + 400Hz HF residual + pullback-tube-acceleration stack on ANYmal-D
Paper proposes the online (timestep-as-task) meta-learned dynamics adaptation formulation as its primary contribution, instantiated as GrBAL/ReBAL.
GrBAL builds on MAML and ReBAL on recurrent meta-learners; the method meta-learns a dynamics prior for fast adaptation.
The method is a model-based meta-RL algorithm: it learns and adapts a forward dynamics model used by a planner.
The adapted dynamics model is used by sampling-based MPC (MPPI in sim, random shooting on the real robot) every timestep.
Online adaptation of the forward model is framed as closely related to online system identification and contrasted with adaptive control.
The control problem is posed as an MDP with a learned stochastic transition (dynamics) model.
Named as an orthogonal, complementary uncertainty mechanism (PETS-style ensembles) the adaptive model could incorporate.
Model-free baselines (TRPO, MAML-RL) are policy-gradient methods used as the sample-efficiency comparison class.

Both adapt a dynamics model online from a short window of recent interaction to control an under-modeled system for goal-reaching; Nagabandi meta-learns a forward-model prior (GrBAL/ReBAL) while IRP learns an observation-conditioned delta-dynamics residual — same online-local-adaptation goal, different mechanism.

Both recover an unknown system from a brief probing interaction and then plan with the specialized model; Nagabandi adapts the forward model from the last M timesteps (implicit, continual), Wiggle-and-Go predicts explicit rope parameters from a fixed wiggle probe (explicit, one-shot).

Both are model-based RL with a learned neural (ensemble/Gaussian) dynamics model trained in simulation and used for planning/branched-rollouts to control robots with sim-to-real transfer; shared MBRL-with-learned-dynamics design family.

Both perform rapid online adaptation of dynamics/policy from recent rollout context: Nagabandi meta-learns a fast-adapting forward model (GrBAL/ReBAL), RAPiD uses RMA-style amortized adaptation modules inferring latent dynamics from recent depth+actions — two instantiations of the 'learn to adapt fast from a short history' recipe.
PETS is built on probabilistic-ensemble
PETS is built on model-based-reinforcement-learning
PETS is built on model-predictive-control
PETS is built on cross-entropy-method
PETS is built on trajectory-optimization
PETS is built on markov-decision-process
PETS introduces trajectory sampling (TS1/TS-infinity) as its particle-based uncertainty-propagation scheme, separating aleatoric vs epistemic uncertainty for planning.

DaXBench's CEM-MPC planning baseline is exactly PETS-style sampling-based MPC optimizing an action sequence over a (learned/differentiable) dynamics model with the cross-entropy method; same distinctive sampling-planning-over-a-model mechanism.

Wiggle-and-Go plans by CMA-ES sampling trajectory optimization over a (system-identified) rope model; same sampling-based trajectory-optimization-over-a-model pattern as PETS's CEM-MPC, with a different sampler (CMA-ES vs CEM) and open-loop vs receding-horizon.

Both are ensemble-dynamics MBRL: Self-Curriculum-MBRL learns a Bi-LSTM probabilistic ensemble dynamics model and uses PETS-style ensemble look-ahead rollouts (and a PETS-style MPC baseline) for DLO shape control; PETS is the probabilistic-ensemble MBRL backbone it cites.

Sibling deep-MBRL method: both learn a neural forward dynamics model and plan with sampling-based MPC for sample-efficient continuous control; Nagabandi et al. explicitly name PETS-style probabilistic ensembles as the orthogonal/complementary uncertainty mechanism their fixed-variance model lacks.

RAPiD's Related Work explicitly revises RMA (Kumar et al. 2021): 'we revise previous works that apply Rapid Motor Adaptation to other robotic tasks... However, effective deformable object manipulation requires not only rapid inference and adaptation to the object's mass and position, but also how the shape of the objects changes, an element missing from these methods. To address this challenge, we revise RAPiD to infer a dynamics embedding of both the deformable object's mass and position and the shape changes.' RAPiD directly adapts RMA's two-phase privileged-teacher + history-regressing-student recipe and adds a particle-position shape encoder.

Both adapt a controller online from a short window of recent interaction, and RMA cites Nagabandi et al. (1803.11347) as prior meta-learning-for-adaptation work. The two are the contrasting flavors of short-recent-context adaptation: RMA amortizes adaptation into a feed-forward context-encoder that regresses a privileged latent (extrinsics) and freezes the policy; GrBAL/ReBAL meta-train a forward dynamics model with a per-timestep gradient/recurrent re-fit and plan with MPC. Distinctive shared mechanism (adapt from last k steps of state-action history), distinct realization.

Both infer an unknown environment/object from a short interaction and then act zero-shot from simulation training. RMA: short proprioceptive history -> low-dim latent (extrinsics) -> act (implicit, amortized). Wiggle-and-Go: short fixed 'wiggle' probe -> explicit 9-D rope parameter vector -> CMA-ES trajectory -> act. Wiggle-and-Go's own related work names RMA a 'close cousin in the privileged-learning lineage' (offline explicit sysID vs online implicit latent). Distinctive shared mechanism (short-probe-then-act for an unidentified system), distinct latent-vs-explicit realization.

Both realize implicit (encoder-based) system identification: encode the task-relevant projection of unknown physics rather than estimating named parameters, then condition the policy on it. RMA regresses an extrinsics latent from a proprioceptive state-action history; IPA folds a fixed-probe trajectory map directly into a ResNet action regressor. Both explicitly argue that predicting exact physics parameters is unnecessary/harmful and that a behavior-relevant implicit encoding suffices.

RMA introduces the extrinsics encoder + adaptation module: regress a low-dimensional privileged environment latent ('extrinsics') from a short proprioceptive state-action history with a single feed-forward pass, in place of test-time parameter optimization. This is the named, reusable mechanism abstracted as amortized-context-encoder-adaptation.

RMA performs implicit system identification: the adaptation module estimates a latent extrinsics vector z_t (not named physics parameters e_t), explicitly arguing that predicting exact parameters is difficult and unnecessary. RMA's SysID baseline (predicting e_t) underperforms RMA (predicting z_t), evidencing the implicit-encoding choice.

Phase 1 privileged teacher (env-factor encoder mu + base policy pi consuming true extrinsics) and Phase 2 non-privileged student (adaptation module phi regressing the extrinsics from proprioceptive history) is a privileged-teacher / non-privileged-student distillation.
RMA is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on the A1 quadruped with no simulation calibration and no real-world fine-tuning, across diverse real terrains.

Phase 1 trains over randomized mass, friction, motor strength, CoM, and a fractal terrain generator; RMA contrasts itself with a pure domain-randomization ('Robust') baseline by adding an adaptation module that reads off where in the randomized distribution the robot currently is.

RMA is positioned against gradient-based meta-learning fast-adaptation (MAML/Finn 2017 and meta-RL descendants, which RMA cites): instead of a meta-learned initialization adapted via test-time rollouts, RMA amortizes adaptation into a supervised context encoder.
Diffuser is a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) whose data are full trajectories; uses epsilon-prediction training and a cosine reverse-covariance schedule.
Reframes trajectory optimization as inference in a reward-perturbed trajectory distribution; planning becomes the probabilistic analogue of argmax over per-timestep rewards.
Diffuser is a new class of deep model-based RL planner that breaks the conventional model/planner abstraction barrier.
Sibling diffusion-for-control formulation; Diffuser models whole (state, action) trajectories for planning and predates/motivates much of the diffusion-policy family for control.
Paper coins and defines planning-as-diffusion: a trajectory-level diffusion model where sampling equals planning, with classifier/cost guidance and inpainting as the planning operators.

Diffuser is the planning-as-diffusion ancestor (guided diffusion over full state+action trajectories); DIDP is the deformable-object instantiation for 3D rope whipping, with PITA's differentiable-physics guidance specializing Diffuser's classifier/cost guidance.

Both attack robust planning over an imperfect learned model and answer model exploitation with two structural defenses: PETS propagates ensemble uncertainty so a gradient-free sampler (CEM-MPC) ignores the untrustworthy far future; Diffuser keeps plans on the data manifold via a generative trajectory prior. Diffuser's intro explicitly names the CEM/random-shooting (PETS-style) regime as the workaround it supersedes.

Title and abstract: extends the existing MMP framework (Noseworthy 2020, Lee EMMP 2023) from discrete-time trajectory representations to parametric curve models (MMP++), adding temporal/via-point modulation and isometric latent regularization (IMMP++).
MMP++ inherits the affine parametric curve models of ProMP/VMP (q(tau;w)=psi(tau)+w*phi(tau)) and the DMP/ProMP/VMP movement-primitive problem setting.
Learning-from-demonstration setting: the manifold and latent density are trained on 5-20 demonstration trajectories per task.
Online iterative replanning is cast as a constrained optimization over the low-dimensional latent state (z', tau') with feasibility and in-distribution constraints; compared against RRT-Connect.

Both plan by generating trajectories from a learned model of the trajectory distribution and keep plans on-manifold/in-distribution; Diffuser uses a diffusion prior with guidance, MMP++ an autoencoder manifold with latent density + constrained latent optimization.
Hindsight relabeling turns every rollout into supervised (goal, action) pairs; the training signal is imitation of the agent's own achieved outcomes (HER/GCSL principle).
The learner is trained by regression/likelihood on relabeled state-action pairs, i.e. iterated behavioral cloning of self-generated data rather than reward maximization.
Family A decodes via-points into minimum-jerk segments per joint; smoothness of the arm command is a property of this basis, not of learning.
A single finite-dimensional parameter vector decoding to a whole trajectory is the movement-primitive formulation; MP_PyTorch is the intended implementation layer.
Duration auto-scaling under velocity/acceleration limits makes every parameter vector executable; oracle probes optimize directly over this parameterization.
Flow matching is the continuous-time sibling of the denoising generative family; used here to model p(w | goal) rather than a point estimate.
The generative model's output space is movement-primitive parameters, not raw action sequences.
Best-of-N sample-and-score is CEM's first iteration without the refit step; the deliberate absence of refitting is what keeps deployment inside the no-online-optimization constraint.
Selection among candidate whole trajectories scored by a model is offline trajectory optimization with a fixed, declared budget.
Coverage-directed search fills under-covered atlas cells with batched CMA-ES populations seeded from pool neighbours (quality-diversity style over a CVT partition).

IRP is the anchor of goal-conditioned dynamic rope manipulation; this idea keeps its low-dimensional swing-primitive framing but replaces per-goal iterative refinement with a zero-shot amortized generator.
DIDP's 84.3% @ 5 cm on 3D rope-whip targeting is the external anchor calibrating the position-marginal of this idea's results.
Closest published match to the target task (zero-shot real 3D rope striking); differs by spending per-goal CMA-ES rather than amortizing, and by targeting position only.
TossingBot supervises a throwing primitive with hindsight outcome labels; this method generalizes that from one label per trajectory to one per timestep.
The planar-casting line establishes supervised inversion of swept sim rollouts; this method keeps the labeling idea and pairs it with a generative head instead of regression.
Free-end-cable casting relabels self-generated rollouts to learn an inverse action map, the direct precursor of the relabel-then-fit pattern used here.
MMP++'s parametric-curve layer is the mechanism actually responsible for its trajectory smoothness; this method adopts that layer directly and omits the latent.
Lost Arc's 3D apex-point action is the canonical compact dynamic-cable parameterization this family generalizes beyond planar shaping.
The conditional manifold shootout arm (B4) is MMP++-derived; this method is the no-autoencoder alternative it is benchmarked against.
Diffuser establishes generative models over whole trajectories as planners; this method applies the same idea to primitive parameters with one-shot sampling instead of iterative denoising.

Wiggle&Go scores candidate trajectories in a calibrated simulator at task time; this method keeps the physics verifier but caps it at a declared best-of-N budget and reports the success-vs-budget curve.
PETS establishes sampling candidate action sequences and scoring them under a model; here the model is the simulator itself, so no learned dynamics or uncertainty propagation is needed.
Addresses two recorded gaps: no rope/DLO method conditions on arrival direction, and none is single-shot open-loop across goals without per-target iteration.
Prior compact parameterizations (apex point, two-arc planar) cannot shape out-of-plane arrival directions; this idea needs a ~30-D smooth family that can, without losing executability.
Deployment ranks candidates with a few-minute-calibrated simulator; whether a mis-calibrated model still ranks correctly is an untested gap in the rapid-adaptation literature.

Extends the MMP framework from discrete-time decoders f(z)->(q_1..q_L) to a continuous-time decoder f(z,t) differentiable in t; the paper names the resulting object a Differentiable Motion Manifold and adopts MMP terminology explicitly (Sec. III-B).

Proposes and names Trajectory Manifold Optimization (Sec. III-D): freeze encoder and latent flow, fine-tune only the decoder on E_{t,tau,z}[J + W^T ReLU(C)^2] with tau ~ U(T); lifts throwing success 17.5 -> 95.8 percent on seen and 4.96 -> 94.1 percent on unseen task parameters.
Training data is generated by solving constrained trajectory optimizations (Adam/SLSQP/COBYLA) per task parameter; TO is also the paper's baseline and the per-query problem TMO amortizes.
The differentiable decoder q(z,t) = sum_b psi^b(z) theta^b(t) is a learned linear basis-function movement primitive; the offline optimizer uses a VMP-style boundary-pinned Gaussian-basis curve model.
Constraint handling is a squared-ReLU penalty method; the constrained per-query problem is recast as a penalized differentiable training objective solved by SGD.

Same sole author; DMMP adopts MMP++'s manifold-of-trajectories formulation and terminology (cited at Sec. III-B for the injective-immersion manifold interpretation) and reuses its boundary-pinned Gaussian-basis parametric curve model as the offline optimizer's parameterization (Eq. 2, B=20).

Sec. III-C states the task-conditioned latent flow p(z|tau) is adopted directly from MMFP; MMFP is also the strongest baseline in Table I (77.4 percent seen SR, collapsing to 15.0 percent unseen) that DMMFP+TMO is measured against.

Extends MMP from fixed-length to variable-length trajectories by making execution horizon L an explicit component of the parameter vector, and replaces the demonstration corpus with 90k planner-generated trajectories: 'Our approach extends motion manifold primitives to variable-length trajectories through a compact parameterization and learns a high-quality manifold from a large-scale dataset of planned motions.'

The latent conditional flow-matching model is trained with the conditioning signal set to 'the actual landing point (x_exe, y_exe) of the executed trajectory measured at z=z_cyl' rather than the commanded target, so the dynamics gap is absorbed implicitly; robustness to a systematic implementation bug is attributed to exactly this ('since our method trains on actual executed landing positions rather than planned targets, the model is robust to this systematic bias').

Goal-manifold sampling + DIMT-RRT + double-simulated-execution repeatability filter yields a 90k-trajectory corpus replacing demonstrations; the dataset-scale ablation quantifies the payoff (parameter-space RMSE 0.201/0.007/0.007/0.001 and length-reconstruction error 12.4%/1.9%/1.1%/0.9% at 0.09k/0.9k/9k/90k).

Residual-style correction scores 93.3% in simulation but 6.7% in the real world, worse than the 10.0pp marginal gain of simply replanning a second time; the paper's diagnostic is that residuals cancel bias but not variance, and target-level residuals are ill-posed because 'distinct trajectories for the same target can yield different landings'.

Argues hand-designed action parameterizations (release pose + twist) cap attainable coordination: 'most methods still rely on manually designed action parameterizations, limiting their ability to produce the highly coordinated motions required in complex tasks'; the paper's own hand-crafted generator reaches only 1.94 m where planning exceeds 2.5 m.

Trajectory parameterization is a via-point movement primitive: cubic Hermite spline boundary term plus K=30 normalized Gaussian RBFs gated by (s(1-s))^2, fit by least squares over positions and velocities.
Latent generative model is conditional flow matching with classifier-free guidance, integrated at inference by the midpoint method over u in [0,1].

Frames the problem as a three-part dynamics gap between planned and executed trajectories (control inaccuracies, contact/release uncertainty, aerodynamic effects) and measures it via sim-vs-real landing distributions at r=1.8 m.
Corpus generation uses DIMT-RRT kinodynamic planning with N_planning=80 samples plus N_smoothing=100 bounded-acceleration shortcut smoothing iterations.

Adopts MMP++'s parametric-curve manifold framework (autoencode curve parameters, not discrete trajectories) and extends it: 'While recent works have extended MMPs to tasks such as tossing, they generally assume fixed-length trajectories, are trained on relatively modest-scale datasets... In contrast, our work extends MMPs to variable-length trajectories via a compact parameterization, learns high-quality manifolds from large-scale planned motion data without requiring downstream post-optimization.'

Directly disputes target-level residual learning for this task class: 'target-level residual learning, as in TossingBot, is unsuitable in our setting since distinct trajectories for the same target can yield different landings; instead, we learn dynamics directly at the trajectory level.' Counter-evidence: a residual-style correction baseline reaches 93.3% in sim but only 6.7% real, vs 60.0% for DA-MMP.

Both attack goal-conditioned dynamic manipulation where the executed outcome deviates from the planned one, from opposite directions: IRP learns delta-dynamics and iterates online per goal; DA-MMP learns a trajectory-level outcome map offline and executes zero-shot open-loop. DA-MMP positions against IRP explicitly in its related-work section.

Both target accurate goal-conditioned throwing under release-timing and control uncertainty; the ETH work answers with a 400 Hz residual policy plus pullback tube acceleration on a legged manipulator, DA-MMP with manifold-based motion generation plus outcome-conditioned flow matching. Cited by DA-MMP as a representative residual-based answer.

Keeps the motion-manifold hypothesis and autoencoder but removes task conditioning from the decoder: the manifold is trained unconditionally and all task dependence moves into a conditional flow-matching vector field over the 3-D latent, which the paper argues (and shows) a shared latent prior + conditional decoder cannot express.

Names and defines 'complex task-motion dependencies' as motion distributions whose mode count or support volume shifts drastically with the task parameter, attributes existing manifold-model failures to the shared latent prior of conditional autoencoders (Sec. 'Limitations of existing motion manifold primitives'), and visualizes the level-1 to level-3 support collapse in a 3-D latent.

Shows DDPM and (Riemannian) flow matching trained directly in trajectory space fail on global high-dimensional trajectories from 10-30 demonstrations: DDPM pouring trajectories do not converge near the cup and RFM output is very jerky (pouring joint accuracy 10.2% and 30.8% vs MMFP 99.9%); also shows latent flow beats latent diffusion on the same manifold (task acc 99.8% vs 81.0-95.0%).
Positions MMFP within the movement-primitive literature (DMP/ProMP/stable-DS/TP-GMM lineage) as a primitive that must encode a diverse trajectory family and generate conditioned on a task parameter.
Trained purely from human demonstrations (10 pouring videos, 30 kinesthetic waving demos) with text annotations; framed as learning-from-demonstration under severe data scarcity.
Uses conditional flow matching (Lipman et al.) as the latent generative model and benchmarks against DDPM/score-SDE both in trajectory space and as latent diffusion variants (VE, VP-1, VP-2).

Same author line and same distinctive mechanism - autoencode a manifold of demonstration trajectories and place a generative model over its low-dimensional latent - but MMP++ autoencodes parametric-curve parameters for modulation while MMFP autoencodes discrete-time trajectories and adds task conditioning via a latent flow; MMFP's conclusion names MMP++'s curve models as the fix for its own fixed-length limitation, and its related-work notes MMP++ does not address task-conditioned generation.

DLO-Lab is a differentiable multi-task deformable-object benchmark in the DaXBench mould, but specialises and materially extends the pattern: it replaces MPM with a customised Discrete-Elastic-Rods solver and adds the three properties Table 1 shows every prior differentiable benchmark lacked -- two-way coupling to rigid bodies and MPM materials, bending plasticity, and closed-loop topology. It keeps the defining bake-off structure (one differentiable simulator, six algorithms across MFRL / FO-MBRL / trajectory optimisation).

The DLO-Lab solver is a differentiable DER: stretching/bending/twisting energies from Bergou et al. 2008/2010 with symplectic Euler time stepping, made differentiable via Taichi autodiff rather than DEFORM's PyTorch + implicit-differentiation route. It extends the concept along three axes -- bending plasticity via a yield threshold and rest-curvature creep rate, closed-loop topology via holonomy correction of the material frames, and gradient checkpointing that makes backward memory independent of horizon length (thousands of steps).

Same architectural pattern with a different pairing: a dedicated rod solver (Taichi DER) coupled two-way into a general-purpose robotics simulator (Genesis rather than Isaac Sim), with impulse-based bidirectional exchange. DLO-Lab extends the pattern in two ways -- the rod solver lives in-tree so gradients flow across the coupling boundary, and coupling reaches MPM continua (fluids, elastoplastics) via Eulerian grid-node impulses, not only rigid bodies. Rigid coupling uses a time-varying SDF with a soft exponential influence factor f = min(exp(d/eps_s), 1).

The paper names and demonstrates the failure mode: in tool-use tasks (Gathering, Lifting, Slingshot) the reward depends on an object the rope has not yet touched, so d(reward)/d(action) is identically zero and gradient descent cannot start. GD lands on the do-nothing reward floor with 0 percent success on all three (Slingshot 6.90 vs CMA-ES 11.07 at 93 percent), while gradient methods win on Unknotting where contact is continuous (SHAC/SAPO approx 46 vs PPO/SAC approx 3). It separates this from the distinct ruggedness/local-optima failure and proposes agent-planned contact initialisation as the fix.

The DLO solver primarily follows Discrete Elastic Rods (Bergou et al. 2008, 2010): centreline vertices plus adapted orthonormal material frames per edge, 3*N_v + N_e DoF, with stretching, bending (curvature binormal) and twisting energies and symplectic Euler time stepping.
Elastic potentials are derived from Kirchhoff's rod model (Dill 1992; O'Reilly 2017), separating strain into stretching, bending and twisting -- the continuum theory DER discretises.

Frictional contact, self-collision and the inextensibility constraint are all resolved with position-based dynamics (Mueller et al. 2007): inverse-mass-weighted geometric projections iterated N_C times, then a velocity-level Coulomb friction update. Chosen over IPC to keep the solve cheap and differentiable.

The entire simulator, 10-task benchmark and agent are scoped to deformable linear objects -- ropes, cables, wires and rubber bands -- and the paper's framing rests on the co-dimensional properties that distinguish DLOs from volumetric deformables.

Two of the six benchmarked methods are trajectory optimisation over an open-loop action sequence: CMA-ES (population 400, sigma0 = 5e-2) and gradient descent through the differentiable simulator (Adam, cosine schedule). CMA-ES is the paper's best method at 86.6 percent average success.

Zero-shot sim-to-real in both regimes: open-loop CMA-ES trajectories deployed unchanged on a Marvin M6 bimanual (Gathering) and an xArm (Wiring-post) after differentiable system identification of rope stiffness from image-mask projection error; and a closed-loop PPO policy trained against a simulated HSV sensor model reaching 7/12 (58 percent) on Wiring-ring.

Both attack the identical concrete problem -- build one differentiable deformable-object simulator, wrap it as a multi-task benchmark, and run a controlled bake-off of gradient-based versus gradient-free policy learning to settle where differentiable physics pays. DLO-Lab cites DaXBench (chen2023daxbench) and scores it directly in its Table 1 (MPM solver: elastic potentials and differentiability yes; bending plasticity, loop topology and coupling no), positioning itself as the DLO-specialised answer. Their conclusions are directly comparable and partly disagree: DLO-Lab finds gradient-free CMA-ES dominant (86.6 percent average success vs 35.0 percent for the best analytic-gradient method).

Both make Discrete Elastic Rods differentiable for robot learning -- a specific shared mechanism, not a generic family. They differ in route: DEFORM uses PyTorch with implicit differentiation through the inner twist optimisation plus a neural residual; DLO-Lab uses Taichi autodiff over an explicit symplectic-Euler DER with gradient checkpointing. Both use the resulting gradients for material-parameter system identification from real observations. DLO-Lab cites DEFORM (chendifferentiable) and scores it in Table 1 as the NN-solver differentiable baseline lacking plasticity, loop topology and coupling.

The two incumbent 3D DLO benchmark-plus-differentiable-simulator papers of 2025-2026, reaching opposite design conclusions on the same problem. DIDP uses a 20-DoF reduced-order GVS model on SoRoSim and argues for a physics-informed diffusion policy; DLO-Lab uses a full-resolution DER solver in Genesis and finds that gradient-free open-loop trajectory optimisation beats learned closed-loop policies under equal budget. Not a citation relationship (DIDP is not in DLO-Lab's bibliography); the edge records that they are directly comparable answers to the same question.

Both build a versatile DLO simulation framework whose defining claim is two-way coupling between a dedicated rod solver and a general-purpose robotics simulator, aimed at robot skill learning: DeformX couples a Cosserat-rod engine into Isaac Sim, DLO-Lab couples a Taichi DER solver into Genesis. The distinguishing contrast is differentiability -- DLO-Lab makes the coupled stack end-to-end differentiable and uses that for both policy optimisation and system identification. Not a citation relationship.

Names 'closed-loop action sequences' as one of three primary technical contributions: predict T_p steps from T_o observations, execute T_a without replanning, then re-infer. Measures the T_a tradeoff directly (interior optimum near 8 steps) and shows the unexecuted surplus buys latency tolerance up to 4 steps under position control.

Does not coin the problem (credits robomimic/IBC/BeT) but formalizes it into short-horizon vs long-horizon multimodality, traces diffusion's multimodality to stochastic initialization plus Langevin noise, shows the score parameterization removes the partition function that destabilizes EBM training, and establishes that position control amplifies multimodality relative to velocity control.

Adopts Janner et al.'s 1-D temporal CNN backbone and modifies it in three named ways: model conditional p(A|O) instead of joint p(A,O), predict action-only rather than concatenated state-action trajectories, and remove inpainting-based goal conditioning as incompatible with a receding prediction horizon. The conditional-vs-joint change is what makes real-time visual conditioning feasible.

DIDP is a goal-conditioned diffusion policy in the Chi et al. class, extended by predicting the full 20-DoF reduced-order rope+arm state instead of actuated joints only, plus an IL+TO finetune and physics-informed test-time adaptation. The DIDP paper's own Related section names Diffusion Policy as 'the policy class DIDP builds on'.
This paper is the origin of the foundation: it defines the diffusion-policy technique class (conditional denoising diffusion over robot action sequences).

The policy is a DDPM: same Langevin denoising update and epsilon-prediction MSE objective, with the output changed to an action chunk and the process conditioned on observations. Uses the iDDPM square-cosine noise schedule and DDIM for inference.
Evaluated entirely under the behavior-cloning formulation and explicitly inherits its limitations (degrades with suboptimal or inadequate demonstrations, cannot exploit negative data).
Positioned as policy learning from demonstration; keywords are 'imitation learning, visuomotor policy, manipulation'.
The contribution is a new form of robot visuomotor policy: end-to-end-trained per-camera ResNet-18 encoders (spatial softmax, GroupNorm) feeding a conditional action denoiser.
Execution borrows receding-horizon control (cited to Mayne & Michalska 1988): commit to T_a of T_p predicted actions, then re-infer, optionally warm-starting from the previous prediction.
Push-T, Transport and ToolHang are the contact-rich, underactuated, high-precision stress cases; Push-T requires exploiting point-contact object dynamics with a circular end-effector.
